大学英语六级考试 2024 年 12 月真题(第二套)
Part I Writing (30 minutes)
Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay that begins with the sentence “Nowadays, more and more students have realized the importance of self-discipline in their personal growth.” You can make comments, cite examples or use your personal experiences to develop your essay. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
You should copy the sentence given in quotes at the beginning of your essay.
Part II Listening Comprehension (30 minutes)
Section A
Directions: In this section, you will hear two long conversations. At the end of each conversation, you will hear four questions. Both the conversation and the questions will be spoken only once. After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices marked A), B), C) and D). Then mark the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 1 with a single line through the centre.

阅读说明：沟通篇改编自 Susan Heitler 于 2020 年的关系沟通建议。对等发言是建议而非所有对话必须各占一半时间的规则，改善效果因关系和情境而异。
Ever been talking about something important with someone you care about and found the discussion frustrating instead of fruitful? Negative energy can then cast a ___26___ over your efforts to build a shared understanding.
In fact, collaborative problem-solving conversations require skills. Strong listening skills are essential. Sprinkling in positivity via appreciation, ___27___ smiles, and warm comments helps. So does the essential ability to keep your emotional tone in the calm zone. If the tone of a dialogue heats up and anger erupts, the dialogue ___28___ from collaborative to adversarial, and progress is likely to come to an immediate ___29___.
In addition, effective dialogue generally has another important characteristic: symmetry.
Symmetry in dialogue refers to the balance of how much each partner talks. Are you each getting equal airtime? When one participant does most of the talking, this asymmetry or lack of balance tends to become annoying to one or both of you.
The silent partner ___30___ tires of only listening, while the talker can feel ___31___. Usually, both would prefer more equal give and take.
Different rates of speech and levels of voice volume can ___32___ symmetry as well. The faster or louder partner can easily begin taking up more airtime. The slower-talking or softer-voiced one can have trouble getting the floor.
Conversations also lose balance when one partner’s opinions count more than the other’s. One person’s input may carry more sway because their style of expression is more ___33___. One viewpoint may tend to get lost because it is expressed more ___34___.
If either partner fairly consistently ___35___ or evaporates, modifying the pattern may be helpful. The dialogue may feel more productive, and at the same time, the relationship overall is likely to feel more positive.

Section B
Directions: In this section, you are going to read a passage with ten statements attached to it. Each statement contains information given in one of the paragraphs. Identify the paragraph from which the information is derived. You may choose a paragraph more than once. Each paragraph is marked with a letter. Answer the questions by marking the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 2.
What Is a Super Blood Wolf Moon?
阅读说明：月亮篇源自 Rachel Feltman 的持续更新文章，题文情景为 2019 年 1 月，现可读网页已更新至 2023 年。此处保留 2019 语境，修正自转、月相、蓝月定义、月食颜色及文化概括；相关匹配题同步修订。
A) Blue moons, rose moons, supermoons. For some reason all the websites seem to think you really want to know all about these moons. “Catch This Weekend’s AMAZING SUPERMOON”, one headline will announce. “The Supermoon Isn’t Actually A Big Deal And You’re All Ruining Astronomy”, another will complain.
B) The latest example is the super blood wolf moon eclipse which sounds like the name of an emotional song I would have performed a modern dance routine to in 9th grade, but is, in fact, an astronomical event that occurred on the night of January 20–21, 2019, depending on the time zone. As we'll explain below, there is nothing supernatural about this moon, and it will not look like a bloody wolf head in the sky or anything wild like that. We get these super lunar events by smashing together all the qualifiers we've historically used to keep track of full moons throughout the year, and in the age of the internet we can get a little too enthusiastic.
C) Consider this your go-to resource for all moon-gazing news. Here’s what you need to know about the latest lunar event.
D) Look, it’s okay if you don’t know. There are probably loads of folks who walk around pretending they totally know why that thing in the sky seems to change its illuminated shape at regular intervals but who totally do not.
E) The moon orbits Earth and is tidally locked: it rotates once on its axis for each orbit, keeping approximately the same face toward us. It shines by reflected sunlight. As it travels around Earth, we see different fractions of its sunlit half. At new moon, it lies in roughly the same direction as the sun and its near side is largely unlit, so it is normally not visible. At full moon, it lies roughly opposite the sun in our sky and the near side is illuminated. Exact alignment can produce an eclipse, but most new and full moons are not eclipses. The far side is not permanently dark. All the other phases are transitions between new and full moon.
F) The moon isn’t always exactly the same distance from Earth, because its orbit isn’t perfectly circular. We call the closest point perigee (近地点), and the most distant point is apogee (远地点). The distance at these points also varies from one orbit to another.
G) The reason you care about this ordinary change in distance is that it turns a moon super. When a full moon happens close to perigee, it's going to look a bit bigger. Honestly, the difference is not that profound, but if you’re in a position to photograph the supermoon next to something that shows the slight increase in scale, it can look pretty cool. The January 2019 eclipse was called super because the full moon occurred near that month’s perigee. The full moon on February 19 was the closest full moon of 2019; this is not a rule that February always has the year’s closest full moon.
H) “Blood moon” commonly refers to a total lunar eclipse. Such an eclipse is not visible from every location every year. Sunlight filtered and bent through Earth’s atmosphere can reach the eclipsed moon, giving it an orange or reddish appearance. The moon can also look orange whenever it's rising or setting, or if it hangs low above the horizon all night --- the light bouncing off of it has to travel along a longer path through the atmosphere there, which scatters more blue light away. The shade varies with atmospheric conditions; a reddish moon is not always an eclipse.
I) A lot of headlines about moons are just ridiculous (you do not need to be particularly excited about a blue moon; it just looks like a regular full moon), but you should definitely roll out of bed to look at a blood moon if one is going to be visible in your region, even though they’re just lunar eclipses and not evidence of bloody battles between the sky gods.
J) In March of 2018, we had our second “blue moon” of the year, to much acclaim. And while that’s not necessarily special in an oh-gosh-get-out-and-look-at-it way, it’s certainly special: a monthly blue moon is the second full moon in a calendar month containing two full moons, and we hadn’t previously had two in one year since 1999. We won’t have it happen again until 2037.
Astronomer David Chapman explained that this is merely a peculiarity of our calendar; once we stopped doing things based on the moon and started trying to follow the sun and the seasons, we stopped having one reliable full moon per month. The moon cycle is 29.53 days long on average, so in most months we still end up with a single new moon and a single full one.
But every once in a while, one month steals a full moon from another. In 2018 (and in 1999, and again in 2037) January and March each had or will have two full moons, while February had or will have none. The calendar dates depend on the time zone; this does not mean February has no moonlight.
K) Getting two blue moons a year is rare, but we have individual blue moons every few years. Also, fun fact: not actually blue. A moon can indeed take on a moody blue color, for example when particles of just the right size disperse through the sky --- and it has nothing to do with the moon’s status as “blue”. Big clouds of ash from volcanic eruptions or fires can do the trick, but it doesn’t happen often, and the stars would certainly have to align for two such rare instances to occur at once.
L) The March 31, 2018 full moon was also described as a Paschal moon. The common explanation connects it with the first full moon of spring and Easter. More precisely, Western Easter is calculated using a tabulated ecclesiastical full moon on or after March 21; that calendar moon and fixed equinox date need not exactly match astronomical events.
M) Sometimes you'll see a headline that promises a moon with so many qualifiers it makes your head spin. A super blue blood worm moon, perhaps? Or a super blood wolf moon? Lots of websites will tell you that “wolf moon” is the traditional name of the first full moon of the year in “Native American” cultures, which is kind of a weird thing to claim given that there are hundreds of distinct Tribal Nations in the US alone, with diverse traditions. The idea that hungry, howling wolves were such a universal constant in January that all of North America with its different cultures, geographies, and languages spontaneously came up with the same nickname is illogical.
N) Many cultures have traditional names for the full moon in a given month or season, so there’s quite a list to draw from if you’re trying to really juice up a story on a slightly-bigger-than-average view of the moon. But these are all based on human calendars and activities and folklore; the name “pink moon” does not mean an April full moon will actually look pink, though I wish it were so.

38. The February 19 full moon was the closest full moon of 2019.
39. The super blood wolf moon has no supernatural meaning and does not resemble a bloody wolf head.
40. A moon low above the horizon can look orange because its reflected light travels a longer path through the atmosphere.

42. As the moon’s orbit is not a hundred-percent circle, its distance from the earth changes.
43. A full moon in a given month or season gets a specific name in different cultures.
44. Some people may pretend to understand why the moon’s illuminated shape changes regularly.

Passage One
Questions 46 to 50 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：乡村篇原作者未能独立追溯，以原 PDF 为底本。文中迁移、住房和能源问题限定为部分地区及所述条件；不能据此断言全球农村皆衰落，或农村居民总碳排放必然更高。
With population increases and urbanisation continuing in many regions, much attention is focused on the sustainability of our cities and scarce attention is paid to the countryside.
Rural life is associated with closely-knit communities, a sense of belonging, and a simple, tranquil life. Yet whilst some or all of these elements exist in the countryside, so do conservatism and a lack of employment opportunities. A shortage of jobs can put pressure on rural communities. In some regions, people move to cities in search of better opportunities, leaving rural settlements less populated. Patterns differ greatly between places.
So how can the countryside ensure its survival among these changes; or should it at all? Due to both the distance between residences and facilities and often intermittent public transport, rural residents may rely more heavily on cars.
Detached rural homes can also require more heating energy than compact urban housing. In the circumstances described here, rural housing and travel can therefore be less energy-efficient. This raises questions about an uncritically idealised rural lifestyle. It does not establish that every rural resident has a larger total carbon footprint: income, consumption, buildings, transport and energy sources all matter.
Protecting the countryside is a hot topic. Those who have made their fortunes in the city often buy second homes in the countryside, visiting intermittently for a sample of a supposedly simple life. The side-effect of this is that increased demand can push up house prices, making homes unaffordable for some local people. This can put further pressure on residents to move away and creates a challenge for local housing policy. For those who believe in rural preservation, this is deplorable.
Whilst an idealised view of the countryside is common, the reality is that rural life has continuously evolved.
Industrialisation brought an increase in divisions of labour, changing social links between rural people. The internet has introduced once foreign cultures into the countryside. Improved travel connections and affordability have made the world more accessible, creating a “global village”. Considering these changes, surely an evolving countryside is inevitable.
Perhaps the countryside should also prepare itself for massive population increases in the future. With cities across the world growing rapidly, how will the current urban generation respond to the inevitable social changes of mass urbanization? Will the longing for a simpler life become stronger, fueling a rural renaissance?
As the world continues to urbanise, the voices calling for rural preservation may well grow louder. Change will continue, with new cities emerging and some existing cities growing into megacities. In the author’s view, the future of the countryside is less clear.

B) It is going to resemble that of cities.
C) It is less likely to stay static.
D) It is less easy to envisage.
Passage Two
Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：审美篇来自 Michael R Spicher 的 2019 年评论，引用 Vessel 等 2018 年研究。实验比较特定样本对图片的评价一致性，不是证明美客观存在或所有文化审美相同。已恢复研究局限，53 题按原研究修正，55 题消除选项重叠。
Statements, like “beauty is in the eye of the beholder (观看者)”, are rarely questioned. They’ve become so embedded in our consciousness that people think it’s absurd to think otherwise. It might be useful, however, to at least push back on this assumption because people evaluate environment, situations, and people aesthetically. We may find that we still believe it is correct, but we may also find that there is a lot more to the situation than you suppose.
A 2018 study in Cognition compared aesthetic responses to images from several domains. Within the samples studied, participants showed more shared taste for faces and natural landscapes than for buildings and artworks. Greater agreement does not mean that the objects received higher average beauty ratings.
The study found that shared taste was most common for faces and natural landscapes, but least common among works of architecture and art. The study did not identify the specific features responsible. Features such as symmetry are possible explanations discussed with reference to earlier research.
Preferences for natural scenes might be learned through life experiences. Factors like habitability, safety, and openness might be preferred as people develop. Some of the details of landscapes change, but the basics are more common, e.g., water, open spaces, and signs of care.
People’s exposure to and expertise in art and architecture vary. The researchers suggest that these differences may contribute to lower shared taste; they did not demonstrate that people simply see fewer buildings than natural spaces.
It’s possible that the lower amount of agreement in the shared taste of artifacts has to do more with elements of style, rather than “behavioral consequences”.
These proposed explanations seem reasonable (or at least possible), but I think there might be an interesting philosophical conclusion that they did not draw. My philosophical interpretation is that there may be an objective basis for some aesthetic preferences. This is not a result directly established by the experiments. I am not saying this would mean beauty is completely objective, just that there could possibly be general objective principles at work, i.e., beauty is not simply in the eye of the beholder.
On this interpretation, nature may exhibit features such as radiance in similar ways in different places. It’s not exactly the same everywhere, but it is common. For example, sunsets can share visual qualities across different places and appeal to many people; this example is not evidence that everyone or every culture has identical preferences.
Possible universal principles of beauty --- such as proportion, fittingness, radiance, and others --- are general categories, which allow for a wide array of embodiments. When people get involved in making artifacts in architecture or art, they apply these very general concepts in unique ways. But the way they applied the principle may not have universal appeal.
This is why it’s important to experience diverse cultures and their artifacts because it opens us up to different ways of approaching or constructing beauty. And it is always good to question our assumptions.
51. How does the author characterize common reactions to the statement “beauty is in the eye of the beholder”?
A) It has hardly ever been disputed.
B) It can be interpreted aesthetically.
C) Many people have found it absurd.
D) People have long been misled by it.
52. Which comparison of shared aesthetic taste did the 2018 study find?
A) Aesthetic tastes tend to differ from person to person.
B) Natural beauty is rarely surpassed by artificial beauty.
C) There is less consensus on objects shaped by human craft.
D) There is general agreement on what is pleasing to the eye.
53. Which possible explanation involving experience does the passage give for differences in people’s appraisal of artifacts?
A) They come out in a great variety of designs.
B) They lead to varying behavioral consequences.
C) They take up much less natural space than landscapes.
D) People differ in their exposure to and expertise in them.
54. What does the author use sunsets to illustrate in his philosophical interpretation?
A) It creates a powerful appeal through its brilliant radiance.
B) It can display similar aesthetic qualities in different places.
C) It embodies beauty with a wide array of aesthetic features.
D) It establishes the principles of beauty in a number of ways.
55. In the author’s interpretation, why might an artifact fail to appeal to everyone?
A) The appreciation of their beauty is not subject to objective standards.
B) The universal principle of beauty prevents a wide array of embodiments.
C) The way their creators apply the principle of beauty may not be pleasing to everybody.
D) Their creators always avoid all general aesthetic principles.

阅读说明：月亮篇源自 Rachel Feltman 的持续更新文章，题文情景为 2019 年 1 月，现可读网页已更新至 2023 年。此处保留 2019 语境，修正自转、月相、蓝月定义、月食颜色及文化概括；相关匹配题同步修订。

A) Blue moons, rose moons, supermoons. For some reason all the websites seem to think you really want to know all about these moons. “Catch This Weekend’s AMAZING SUPERMOON”, one headline will announce. “The Supermoon Isn’t Actually A Big Deal And You’re All Ruining Astronomy”, another will complain.

B) The latest example is the super blood wolf moon eclipse which sounds like the name of an emotional song I would have performed a modern dance routine to in 9th grade, but is, in fact, an astronomical event that occurred on the night of January 20–21, 2019, depending on the time zone. As we'll explain below, there is nothing supernatural about this moon, and it will not look like a bloody wolf head in the sky or anything wild like that. We get these super lunar events by smashing together all the qualifiers we've historically used to keep track of full moons throughout the year, and in the age of the internet we can get a little too enthusiastic.
C) Consider this your go-to resource for all moon-gazing news. Here’s what you need to know about the latest lunar event.

D) Look, it’s okay if you don’t know. There are probably loads of folks who walk around pretending they totally know why that thing in the sky seems to change its illuminated shape at regular intervals but who totally do not.

E) The moon orbits Earth and is tidally locked: it rotates once on its axis for each orbit, keeping approximately the same face toward us. It shines by reflected sunlight. As it travels around Earth, we see different fractions of its sunlit half. At new moon, it lies in roughly the same direction as the sun and its near side is largely unlit, so it is normally not visible. At full moon, it lies roughly opposite the sun in our sky and the near side is illuminated. Exact alignment can produce an eclipse, but most new and full moons are not eclipses. The far side is not permanently dark. All the other phases are transitions between new and full moon.

F) The moon isn’t always exactly the same distance from Earth, because its orbit isn’t perfectly circular. We call the closest point perigee (近地点), and the most distant point is apogee (远地点). The distance at these points also varies from one orbit to another.

G) The reason you care about this ordinary change in distance is that it turns a moon super. When a full moon happens close to perigee, it's going to look a bit bigger. Honestly, the difference is not that profound, but if you’re in a position to photograph the supermoon next to something that shows the slight increase in scale, it can look pretty cool. The January 2019 eclipse was called super because the full moon occurred near that month’s perigee. The full moon on February 19 was the closest full moon of 2019; this is not a rule that February always has the year’s closest full moon.

H) “Blood moon” commonly refers to a total lunar eclipse. Such an eclipse is not visible from every location every year. Sunlight filtered and bent through Earth’s atmosphere can reach the eclipsed moon, giving it an orange or reddish appearance. The moon can also look orange whenever it's rising or setting, or if it hangs low above the horizon all night --- the light bouncing off of it has to travel along a longer path through the atmosphere there, which scatters more blue light away. The shade varies with atmospheric conditions; a reddish moon is not always an eclipse.

I) A lot of headlines about moons are just ridiculous (you do not need to be particularly excited about a blue moon; it just looks like a regular full moon), but you should definitely roll out of bed to look at a blood moon if one is going to be visible in your region, even though they’re just lunar eclipses and not evidence of bloody battles between the sky gods.

J) In March of 2018, we had our second “blue moon” of the year, to much acclaim. And while that’s not necessarily special in an oh-gosh-get-out-and-look-at-it way, it’s certainly special: a monthly blue moon is the second full moon in a calendar month containing two full moons, and we hadn’t previously had two in one year since 1999. We won’t have it happen again until 2037.

Astronomer David Chapman explained that this is merely a peculiarity of our calendar; once we stopped doing things based on the moon and started trying to follow the sun and the seasons, we stopped having one reliable full moon per month. The moon cycle is 29.53 days long on average, so in most months we still end up with a single new moon and a single full one.

But every once in a while, one month steals a full moon from another. In 2018 (and in 1999, and again in 2037) January and March each had or will have two full moons, while February had or will have none. The calendar dates depend on the time zone; this does not mean February has no moonlight.

K) Getting two blue moons a year is rare, but we have individual blue moons every few years. Also, fun fact: not actually blue. A moon can indeed take on a moody blue color, for example when particles of just the right size disperse through the sky --- and it has nothing to do with the moon’s status as “blue”. Big clouds of ash from volcanic eruptions or fires can do the trick, but it doesn’t happen often, and the stars would certainly have to align for two such rare instances to occur at once.

L) The March 31, 2018 full moon was also described as a Paschal moon. The common explanation connects it with the first full moon of spring and Easter. More precisely, Western Easter is calculated using a tabulated ecclesiastical full moon on or after March 21; that calendar moon and fixed equinox date need not exactly match astronomical events.

M) Sometimes you'll see a headline that promises a moon with so many qualifiers it makes your head spin. A super blue blood worm moon, perhaps? Or a super blood wolf moon? Lots of websites will tell you that “wolf moon” is the traditional name of the first full moon of the year in “Native American” cultures, which is kind of a weird thing to claim given that there are hundreds of distinct Tribal Nations in the US alone, with diverse traditions. The idea that hungry, howling wolves were such a universal constant in January that all of North America with its different cultures, geographies, and languages spontaneously came up with the same nickname is illogical.

N) Many cultures have traditional names for the full moon in a given month or season, so there’s quite a list to draw from if you’re trying to really juice up a story on a slightly-bigger-than-average view of the moon. But these are all based on human calendars and activities and folklore; the name “pink moon” does not mean an April full moon will actually look pink, though I wish it were so.

阅读说明：乡村篇原作者未能独立追溯，以原 PDF 为底本。文中迁移、住房和能源问题限定为部分地区及所述条件；不能据此断言全球农村皆衰落，或农村居民总碳排放必然更高。
With population increases and urbanisation continuing in many regions, much attention is focused on the sustainability of our cities and scarce attention is paid to the countryside.

Rural life is associated with closely-knit communities, a sense of belonging, and a simple, tranquil life. Yet whilst some or all of these elements exist in the countryside, so do conservatism and a lack of employment opportunities. A shortage of jobs can put pressure on rural communities. In some regions, people move to cities in search of better opportunities, leaving rural settlements less populated. Patterns differ greatly between places.

So how can the countryside ensure its survival among these changes; or should it at all? Due to both the distance between residences and facilities and often intermittent public transport, rural residents may rely more heavily on cars.

Detached rural homes can also require more heating energy than compact urban housing. In the circumstances described here, rural housing and travel can therefore be less energy-efficient. This raises questions about an uncritically idealised rural lifestyle. It does not establish that every rural resident has a larger total carbon footprint: income, consumption, buildings, transport and energy sources all matter.

Protecting the countryside is a hot topic. Those who have made their fortunes in the city often buy second homes in the countryside, visiting intermittently for a sample of a supposedly simple life. The side-effect of this is that increased demand can push up house prices, making homes unaffordable for some local people. This can put further pressure on residents to move away and creates a challenge for local housing policy. For those who believe in rural preservation, this is deplorable.
Whilst an idealised view of the countryside is common, the reality is that rural life has continuously evolved.

Industrialisation brought an increase in divisions of labour, changing social links between rural people. The internet has introduced once foreign cultures into the countryside. Improved travel connections and affordability have made the world more accessible, creating a “global village”. Considering these changes, surely an evolving countryside is inevitable.

Perhaps the countryside should also prepare itself for massive population increases in the future. With cities across the world growing rapidly, how will the current urban generation respond to the inevitable social changes of mass urbanization? Will the longing for a simpler life become stronger, fueling a rural renaissance?

As the world continues to urbanise, the voices calling for rural preservation may well grow louder. Change will continue, with new cities emerging and some existing cities growing into megacities. In the author’s view, the future of the countryside is less clear.

B) It will present an idealised way of life.

B) It is going to resemble that of cities.
C) It is less likely to stay static.

Passage Two
Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：审美篇来自 Michael R Spicher 的 2019 年评论，引用 Vessel 等 2018 年研究。实验比较特定样本对图片的评价一致性，不是证明美客观存在或所有文化审美相同。已恢复研究局限，53 题按原研究修正，55 题消除选项重叠。

Statements, like “beauty is in the eye of the beholder (观看者)”, are rarely questioned. They’ve become so embedded in our consciousness that people think it’s absurd to think otherwise. It might be useful, however, to at least push back on this assumption because people evaluate environment, situations, and people aesthetically. We may find that we still believe it is correct, but we may also find that there is a lot more to the situation than you suppose.

A 2018 study in Cognition compared aesthetic responses to images from several domains. Within the samples studied, participants showed more shared taste for faces and natural landscapes than for buildings and artworks. Greater agreement does not mean that the objects received higher average beauty ratings.

The study found that shared taste was most common for faces and natural landscapes, but least common among works of architecture and art. The study did not identify the specific features responsible. Features such as symmetry are possible explanations discussed with reference to earlier research.

Preferences for natural scenes might be learned through life experiences. Factors like habitability, safety, and openness might be preferred as people develop. Some of the details of landscapes change, but the basics are more common, e.g., water, open spaces, and signs of care.

People’s exposure to and expertise in art and architecture vary. The researchers suggest that these differences may contribute to lower shared taste; they did not demonstrate that people simply see fewer buildings than natural spaces.
It’s possible that the lower amount of agreement in the shared taste of artifacts has to do more with elements of style, rather than “behavioral consequences”.

These proposed explanations seem reasonable (or at least possible), but I think there might be an interesting philosophical conclusion that they did not draw. My philosophical interpretation is that there may be an objective basis for some aesthetic preferences. This is not a result directly established by the experiments. I am not saying this would mean beauty is completely objective, just that there could possibly be general objective principles at work, i.e., beauty is not simply in the eye of the beholder.

On this interpretation, nature may exhibit features such as radiance in similar ways in different places. It’s not exactly the same everywhere, but it is common. For example, sunsets can share visual qualities across different places and appeal to many people; this example is not evidence that everyone or every culture has identical preferences.

Possible universal principles of beauty --- such as proportion, fittingness, radiance, and others --- are general categories, which allow for a wide array of embodiments. When people get involved in making artifacts in architecture or art, they apply these very general concepts in unique ways. But the way they applied the principle may not have universal appeal.

This is why it’s important to experience diverse cultures and their artifacts because it opens us up to different ways of approaching or constructing beauty. And it is always good to question our assumptions.

51. How does the author characterize common reactions to the statement “beauty is in the eye of the beholder”?
A) It has hardly ever been disputed.
B) It can be interpreted aesthetically.
C) Many people have found it absurd.
D) People have long been misled by it.

A) Aesthetic tastes tend to differ from person to person.
B) Natural beauty is rarely surpassed by artificial beauty.
C) There is less consensus on objects shaped by human craft.
D) There is general agreement on what is pleasing to the eye.

A) They come out in a great variety of designs.
B) They lead to varying behavioral consequences.
C) They take up much less natural space than landscapes.
D) People differ in their exposure to and expertise in them.

A) It creates a powerful appeal through its brilliant radiance.
B) It can display similar aesthetic qualities in different places.
C) It embodies beauty with a wide array of aesthetic features.
D) It establishes the principles of beauty in a number of ways.

55. In the author’s interpretation, why might an artifact fail to appeal to everyone?
A) The appreciation of their beauty is not subject to objective standards.
B) The universal principle of beauty prevents a wide array of embodiments.
C) The way their creators apply the principle of beauty may not be pleasing to everybody.
D) Their creators always avoid all general aesthetic principles.

Astronomer David Chapman explained that this is merely a peculiarity of our calendar; once we stopped doing things based on the moon and started trying to follow the sun and the seasons, we stopped ha ving one reliable full moon per month. H) Blood moons only occur during total lunar eclipses (which can happe n a few times a year in any given location). When the moon slips through our shadow, we give it a reddish coloring.
